brief: Intro to "RAG vs fine-tuning" explainer; positions RAG for freshness/citations, fine-tuning for style/latency; mentions a 100k-doc support-KB use case.
facts: RAG positioned for freshness and citations
Fine-tuning positioned for style and latency
original_draft:
In today's rapidly evolving AI landscape, few debates come up more often than RAG versus fine-tuning. Both approaches promise to make large language models more useful for your specific needs — but they solve fundamentally different problems, and choosing the wrong one can cost you time, money, and accuracy.

At a high level, the distinction is straightforward. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) shines when you need freshness and citations: because it pulls answers from a live knowledge base at query time, your model can reference up-to-date documents and point users to exact sources. Fine-tuning, on the other hand, excels at style and latency — it bakes knowledge and tone directly into the model's weights, delivering faster, more consistent responses without a retrieval step.

Consider a real-world example: a customer-support knowledge base with 100,000 documents. Should you retrieve from it, fine-tune on it, or both? The answer, as we'll see, depends on how often your content changes, how much citations matter, and what latency your users will tolerate.

In this post, we'll break down the trade-offs, explore when to use each approach, and help you make the right call for your use case. Let's dive in.

Because it pulls answers from a live knowledge base at query time, the model can reference documents that changed yesterday and point users to exact sources. Fine-tuning is for style and latency. It bakes knowledge and tone into the model's weights, so responses come back faster and more consistent, with no retrieval step.

The example that makes the trade-off concrete: a customer-support knowledge base with 100,000 documents. Do you retrieve from it, fine-tune on it, or both? brief: Intro to a post on Postgres indexing pitfalls; covers unused indexes bloating writes; one client had 23 indexes on one table, write throughput doubled after dropping 14.
facts: Client had 23 indexes on one table
Write throughput doubled after dropping 14 indexes
original_draft:
When it comes to Postgres performance, indexes are often treated as a silver bullet. Need a faster query? Add an index. But here's the thing: every index you add comes with a hidden cost, and over time, those costs can quietly erode your database's write performance.

Unused indexes are one of the most common — and most overlooked — pitfalls. Every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE has to maintain every index on the table, which means indexes that never serve a single query are still bloating your writes, inflating your storage, and slowing down your vacuum cycles.

We saw this firsthand with a recent client. One of their core tables had accumulated 23 indexes over the years. After a careful audit, we dropped 14 of them — and write throughput doubled. No hardware changes, no query rewrites, just less unnecessary work on every write.

In this post, we'll walk through the most common Postgres indexing pitfalls, show you how to identify unused indexes in your own database, and share a practical checklist for keeping your indexes lean. Whether you're running a small side project or a high-traffic production system, there's something here for you. Let's get started.

brief: Intro to remote-onboarding guide; company onboarded 27 remote hires in one year; time-to-first-PR cut from 12 days to 5.

Over the past year, we onboarded 27 remote hires. Along the way, we made plenty of mistakes, ran plenty of experiments, and learned what actually moves the needle. The result? We cut our time-to-first-PR from 12 days to just 5 — meaning new engineers are shipping meaningful code in their first week instead of their third.

In this guide, we'll share the exact playbook that got us there: how we structure the first day, the role of onboarding buddies, the documentation that matters (and the documentation that doesn't), and the metrics we track to keep improving.

Whether you're onboarding your first remote hire or your fiftieth, we hope these lessons help you build a smoother, faster, and more welcoming experience for every new teammate. Because great onboarding isn't just an HR checkbox — it's your first, best chance to show new hires how your team really works. Let's dive in.

brief: Intro to "The State of Design Systems 2026" report; survey of 412 designers; 61% say their design system is partially adopted at best.
facts: 61% say their design system is partially adopted at best
original_draft:
Design systems have become a cornerstone of modern product development — but how are they actually faring inside organizations? To find out, we surveyed 412 designers across industries, company sizes, and levels of design maturity for The State of Design Systems 2026.

The headline finding is a sobering one: 61% of respondents say their design system is partially adopted at best. In other words, for the majority of teams, the design system exists — but it isn't yet the single source of truth it was meant to be.

Why does adoption stall? The reasons are varied: unclear ownership, competing priorities, gaps between design and code, and the ever-present challenge of keeping documentation up to date. But the data also points to what's working — and the teams that get adoption right share some surprisingly consistent habits.

In this report, we'll unpack the numbers, highlight the trends shaping design systems in 2026, and share practical takeaways you can bring back to your own team. Whether you're just launching your first component library or scaling a mature system across dozens of products, there's something here for you. Let's take a closer look at what the data tells us.

brief: Personal-finance post on emergency funds; recommends 3–6 months of expenses; author built theirs in 14 months on a $52k salary.
facts: Author built their emergency fund in 14 months
original_draft:
Let's be honest: building an emergency fund isn't glamorous. There's no dopamine hit, no compounding chart to admire, no one bragging about their savings account at parties. And yet, if there's one financial move that consistently pays off, it's this one.

The standard advice is to set aside 3–6 months of expenses — enough of a cushion to absorb a job loss, a medical bill, or a surprise car repair without reaching for a credit card. It sounds simple. It's also, for most people, genuinely hard.

I know because I've done it. It took me 14 months to build my emergency fund on a $52k salary, and along the way I learned that the challenge is less about math and more about habits, trade-offs, and staying motivated when progress feels painfully slow.

In this post, I'll share exactly how I did it: the budget changes that mattered most, the automation that kept me consistent, and the mindset shifts that made all the difference. If you've been putting off starting your emergency fund — or you've started and stalled — I hope this gives you a realistic roadmap, and the nudge to begin today. Future you will thank you.

brief: Travel post on 4 days in Kyoto; stayed in Gion; highlights Fushimi Inari at 6am and a kaiseki dinner that cost ¥18,000.

There's something magical about Kyoto. The ancient temples, the quiet lanes, the sense that every corner holds a thousand years of history — it's a city that rewards slowing down, even when you only have four days.

That's exactly what we had: four days to soak in as much of Kyoto as possible. We based ourselves in Gion, the city's famous geisha district, where wooden machiya houses and lantern-lit streets make even a simple evening stroll feel like stepping back in time.

The highlights? Walking beneath the vermilion gates of Fushimi Inari at 6am, before the crowds arrived, with the mountain path almost entirely to ourselves. And on our final night, a kaiseki dinner that cost ¥18,000 — not cheap, but an unforgettable procession of seasonal dishes that felt more like art than food.

In this post, I'll walk you through our full four-day itinerary: where we stayed, what we ate, what we'd happily skip next time, and the small tips that made the trip smoother. Whether it's your first visit to Kyoto or your fifth, I hope this guide helps you plan an unforgettable adventure of your own. Let's get into it.

The numbers tell the story: the average mid-market company uses 7 different tools just for purchasing, from spreadsheets and email threads to ERP modules and standalone approval apps.

The result is a process nobody loves. Requests get lost between systems. Approvers don't know what's waiting for them. Finance loses visibility into committed spend. And what should be a simple purchase turns into a multi-week ordeal that frustrates everyone involved.

It doesn't have to be this way. Modern procurement software consolidates requests, approvals, and vendor management into a single streamlined workflow — and the impact can be dramatic. Companies that make the switch routinely see 14-day approval cycles drop to just 3, freeing their teams to focus on strategy instead of status-chasing.

In this post, we'll explore why procurement tooling has become so fragmented, what a consolidated approach looks like in practice, and how to evaluate whether your organization is ready to make the change. If your team is drowning in purchasing busywork, keep reading — there's a better way. Let's take a closer look.

brief: Engineering postmortem-style post on a 4-hour outage caused by an expired TLS cert on an internal service; 3 action items.
facts: Caused by an expired TLS certificate on an internal service
original_draft:
On Tuesday, our platform experienced a 4-hour outage that affected a significant portion of our users. The root cause: an expired TLS certificate on an internal service that sat squarely in our request path. We know how disruptive this was, and we're sharing this postmortem in the spirit of transparency — both to explain what happened and to outline what we're changing.

The short version is humbling. A certificate we didn't realize was close to expiry, on a service most of us rarely thought about, expired quietly — and took a surprising amount of our stack down with it. Alerts fired, but the failure mode was confusing, and it took longer than it should have to trace the cascading errors back to their source.
